title: The Vanishing Aral Sea
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Until the 1960s, the Aral Sea in Central Asia was the fourth largest lake in the world, with an area of about sixty-eight thousand square kilometres, roughly the size of Ireland. It lay between what are now Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan and was fed by two great rivers, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, which carry melted snow from the mountains far to the south and east. Fishing boats worked its waters, and the port towns on its shores were prosperous.

The change began when Soviet planners decided to turn the dry land around the sea into cotton fields. They dug thousands of kilometres of canals to carry water from the two rivers to the crops. Many of the canals were unlined, so a large share of the water soaked into the ground or evaporated before it reached the fields. Cotton also needs a great deal of water. By the 1980s, in most years, almost nothing was left of the rivers by the time they reached the sea.

The sea responded by shrinking. By 1987 it had divided into two separate parts, a small northern lake and a larger southern one, and by 2007 it had lost about ninety per cent of its original area. As the water fell, the remaining water became saltier, and the native fish could not survive. The fishing industry, which had once employed tens of thousands of people, collapsed. The old port of Moynaq is now many kilometres from the water, and the rusting hulks of ships lie half buried in the sand.

The consequences reached far beyond the fishing villages. The exposed seabed is covered with salt, as well as with chemical residues from the fertilisers and pesticides that drained from the cotton fields over the years. Strong winds lift this material into the air and carry it for hundreds of kilometres. Doctors in the region report high rates of throat and lung disease. The climate has also changed: without the sea to moderate the temperature, the summers are hotter and the winters colder than they once were.

In the north, a more hopeful story has unfolded. In 2005 Kazakhstan completed the Kok-Aral dam, a barrier across the channel that separates the northern lake from the southern one. Water from the Syr Darya, which once drained away south, now stays in the north. Within a few years the level had risen, the salt content had fallen, and the fish had returned. The catch has grown steadily, and the shoreline has moved back towards the town of Aralsk.

The southern part of the sea has not been so fortunate. Most scientists agree that it cannot be restored, because the water that would be needed is now used for farming, and there is no political will to give it up. Efforts have therefore concentrated on limiting the damage. In Uzbekistan, workers have planted saxaul, a hardy desert shrub, over large areas of the dry seabed, now called the Aralkum desert, in order to hold the soil in place and reduce the dust. Some communities have also turned to new work, such as raising livestock or taking part in the search for oil and gas.

The Aral Sea has become a warning to the world. It shows how quickly a large body of water can disappear when too much is taken from the rivers that feed it, and how hard it is to reverse the damage afterwards. Farmers in the region are now being encouraged to line canals, to use drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to the roots of plants, and to grow crops that need less water than cotton. Such measures are expensive, but supporters argue that they cost far less than the damage that the disappearance of the sea has caused.

items.s: The Aral Sea was once the fourth largest lake in the world.
e: the fourth largest lake in the world

items.s: The Aral Sea was fed by three major rivers.
e: two great rivers, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya

items.s: Soviet planners wanted to grow cotton on dry land near the sea.
e: turn the dry land around the sea into cotton fields

items.s: Most of the canals were lined to prevent water loss.
e: Many of the canals were unlined

items.s: By 1987 the sea had split into two parts.
e: By 1987 it had divided into two separate parts

items.s: Native fish were killed by chemicals dumped by factories.
e: the remaining water became saltier, and the native fish could not survive

items.s: The port of Moynaq is now far from the water.
e: now many kilometres from the water

items.s: Dust from the seabed has been blown as far as the Arctic.
e: carry it for hundreds of kilometres
items.w: The passage says dust travels hundreds of kilometres but names no destination.

items.s: Summers in the region are now cooler than they were.
e: the summers are hotter and the winters colder

items.s: The Kok-Aral dam was completed in 2005.
e: In 2005 Kazakhstan completed the Kok-Aral dam

items.s: Experts believe the southern sea can be restored within ten years.
Closing the Kok-Aral dam has benefited the northern lake.
e: the level had risen, the salt content had fallen, and the fish had returned

items.s: The southern sea could easily be refilled if politicians wished.
e: there is no political will to give it up

items.s: Cotton is a crop that uses little water.
e: Cotton also needs a great deal of water

items.s: Measures to save water in farming are cheaper than the damage done by the loss of the sea.
e: supporters argue that they cost far less than the damage
items.w: The writer reports what supporters argue and does not give a personal view.

items.s: The disappearance of the sea is a lesson for other parts of the world.
e: The Aral Sea has become a warning to the world

items.s: Planting saxaul has completely solved the dust problem.
e: in order to hold the soil in place and reduce the dust

items.q: Why was so much canal water lost before it reached the cotton fields?
o: The rivers were frozen in winter.
Farmers took too much from each canal.
e: Many of the canals were unlined

items.q: What happened to the fishing industry as the sea shrank?
o: It was replaced by fish farming.
e: The fishing industry, which had once employed tens of thousands of people, collapsed

items.q: Why does the writer describe the north as a more hopeful story?
o: The northern lake has recovered in several ways.
The Syr Darya has been refilled completely.
The town of Aralsk has been rebuilt.
The dam has been copied in the south.
e: the level had risen, the salt content had fallen, and the fish had returned

groups.qt: Which TWO health or climate effects are mentioned in paragraph D?
o: Throat and lung disease is common.
e: high rates of throat and lung disease
